title: Irregular CPU load spikes with HAProxy 2.7.2
body: After upgrading our HAProxy load balancers from 2.6.7 to 2.7.2, CPU usage became highly irregular even though requests, sessions, and connection metrics did not change significantly. Individual HAProxy processes sometimes consume more than 300% CPU, and each roughly 25% jump corresponds to one core on our four-core VMs. We run one four-thread HAProxy worker and reload with SIGUSR2 when updating the crt-list, so old processes may coexist, but a single process can exhibit the spike by itself while the CLI still reports more than 50% idle. Perf shows substantial crypto and scheduler-related activity. The pattern is strongest on Azure but appears on other providers. An isolated Jammy/OpenSSL 3 deployment still used about 80% per core but did not reproduce the production spike pattern.

symptoms_visible: Since upgrading from HAProxy 2.6.7 to 2.7.2, CPU usage moves between irregular levels and sometimes reaches 100% on all four cores even though request, session, and connection rates remain similar.
A single HAProxy process can consume more than 300% CPU while its CLI reports Idle_pct above 50%.
My isolated Jammy/OpenSSL 3 deployment used around 80% per core but did not show the production load pattern.
N0.label: N0 irregular production CPU spikes reported

symptoms_visible: The selected HAProxy process continues to occupy a full core even though its two CLI samples ten seconds apart show Idle_pct 78 and very little current traffic.
N1.label: N1 activity counters captured

symptoms_visible: During a spike, strace repeatedly prints clock_gettime calls and epoll_wait calls that immediately return with no events.
HATop shows hundreds or more than a thousand tasks and file descriptors while only about 80 requests per second are arriving.
Only one current HAProxy process consumes the CPU; any older processes contribute little, and the same behavior occurs with only one worker process.
We also see more 504 responses with the sH-- termination state during the spikes.
N2.label: N2 spinning-worker evidence collected

symptoms_visible: The CPU remains pinned in one or two current workers; old workers do not consume significant CPU, and the spike also occurs when only one worker process remains.
N2_x.label: N2_x old-worker theory aftermath

symptoms_visible: After reverting the deployment to HAProxy 2.6.9, the irregular CPU levels and pinned-core behavior are gone and the load graph is stable again.
N3.label: N3 rollback removes the production symptom

symptoms_visible: After upgrading production to HAProxy 2.7.5, our CPU load pattern looks normal and the irregular pinned-core spikes no longer occur.
N_terminal.label: terminal fixed release verified in production

question_patterns: Can you capture 'show info; show activity' twice ten seconds apart from a process that is consuming a core?
Please collect two CLI activity snapshots from the affected worker so we can compare its wakeups, run queue, loops, and SSL counters.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I selected the HAProxy process that was hogging a full core and ran the two CLI queries ten seconds apart. Both samples show Idle_pct 78. The first activity block includes ctxsw 710947051, long_rq 97104348, loops 97589409 and wake_tasks 97169744; ten seconds later those values are 715847225, 97773213, 98261358 and 97833583. I don't have comparable live data from the older version and don't really understand what these counters are telling me.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The counters barely change during the ten-second interval, while SSL handshake and accepted-connection counters rise in proportion to the CPU use.
The same very rapid growth appears when I sample for twenty seconds instead of ten.

edges.comment: Issue c2-c3, reporter's HAProxy 2.7.2 production process: participant2 requested paired CLI measurements and the reporter pasted the raw counters without interpreting them.

question_patterns: While the CPU is pinned, can you run 'show tasks' several times and paste the function names and counts?
Please capture the task listing from the affected worker during a spike.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran it several times at 100% CPU. The output alternates between small sets containing h1_io_cb, ssl_sock_io_cb and sc_conn_io_cb, with occasional accept_queue_process and process_stream entries. In another capture it reported 31 active tasks even though little traffic was arriving.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The task listing is dominated by health-check tasks belonging to old stopping workers, and the current worker has no H1, SSL, or connection callbacks running.
The exact task count varies between captures, but the same H1, SSL, and connection callback names recur.

question_patterns: Can you send 'show fd' and an anonymized 'show sess all' from the affected process?
Please run 'set anon on' and collect the file-descriptor and session dumps while the worker is exhibiting the problem.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I collected show fd and anonymized show sess all dumps from the affected workers. One later capture had more than 1,400 file descriptors and HATop showed over 1,800 tasks while one process was hogging CPU. I also repeated both dumps on a VM with only a single worker process when about two dozen HAProxy VMs were pinned at 100%.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The dumps show only normal idle listeners and no active or errored H1/SSL frontend connections during the CPU spike.

edges.comment: Issue c4-c17 and c20, affected production systems operated by participant3 and the reporter, folded into one simulated user side. The strace, low-traffic HATop observations, timeout reports, and single-worker reproduction were volunteered around the requested show-tasks/show-fd/show-sess captures. The raw dumps remain user evidence; participant2's later correlation of 31 errored connections with 31 active FD tasks is engineer-side inference.

solution.intent: Attribute the CPU usage to frequent reloads leaving old workers that continue running backend health checks.
solution.concrete_example: Reduce reload frequency or terminate old workers because accumulated stopping processes may continue running backend health checks and consume the CPU.

edges.comment: Issue c18-c20: participant4 suggested the old-worker health-check problem from issue 1874. Participant3 and the reporter rejected it with production evidence: old workers remained quiet, while one current worker consumed the CPU, including on a VM with only one worker process.

solution.intent: Temporarily roll production back to the known-stable HAProxy 2.6 line to stop the CPU spikes while the 2.7 defect is diagnosed.
solution.concrete_example: Revert the affected deployment to HAProxy 2.6.9 and monitor whether the CPU graph returns to its earlier stable pattern.

edges.comment: Issue c21: participant3 reported that the affected deployment reverted to 2.6.9 and the irregular CPU pattern disappeared. This is an effective production mitigation, not the eventual 2.7 fix.

solution.intent: After the old-worker theory is contradicted, temporarily roll production back to the known-stable HAProxy 2.6 line while the current-worker spin is diagnosed.
solution.concrete_example: Since the spike occurs with one current worker and the old processes remain quiet, revert the deployment to HAProxy 2.6.9 and monitor the CPU graph.

edges.comment: Recovery from the falsified c18 hypothesis using the actual c21 rollback performed by the affected operator.

solution.intent: Deploy a fixed HAProxy 2.7 build containing the H1 multiplexer error-handling correction, which stops errored TLS/H1 connections from remaining runnable and spinning, then verify the production CPU pattern.
solution.concrete_example: The FD and session dumps led maintainers to connections with transport errors that remained active. A pure SSL error could set the connection error without the corresponding socket shutdown state, leaving the H1 side waiting while callbacks repeatedly woke. Install HAProxy 2.7.5, which contains the H1 multiplexer fix, and verify the CPU graph under normal production traffic.
solution.inference_hint: Maintainers correlated the show-task count with 31 errored frontend H1/SSL connections in the FD dump. They inferred that a pure SSL error could leave the raw socket alive without read/write shutdown flags: the H1 multiplexer observed an error and waited, while the connection layer performed no further work, producing repeated runnable callbacks. A maintainer reproduced this with a hacked trace filter, first validated an ssl_sock shutdown-flag patch, and then shipped the proper fix in the H1 multiplexer. These conclusions were not stated by the reporter.

edges.comment: Issue c26-c42: participant2 and participant6 derived the connection-state correlation, reproduced the defect synthetically, and fixed the H1 multiplexer. The affected operator declined an untested production patch, waited for the normal release, then participant8 confirmed that the production load pattern was good after upgrading to 2.7.5; affected operators are folded into one user side. The crashes reported from 2.7.6 in c44 onward were explicitly declared unrelated in c50 and belong to a separate issue, so they are excluded from this diagnostic chain.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: an SSL transport error could leave an H1 connection without the corresponding socket shutdown state, so the H1 multiplexer waited while connection callbacks repeatedly woke and consumed a core.
Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected activity, task, FD, session, and strace evidence, including the recurring H1/SSL/connection callbacks and errored frontend connections during low traffic.

Must not attribute the primary spike to accumulated old workers or their health checks; the affected operators observed one current worker consuming the CPU while old workers remained quiet, including on a single-worker VM.
A rollback to the stable 2.6 deployment may be offered as a temporary mitigation, but the durable resolution is a fixed 2.7 build containing the H1 multiplexer error-handling correction.
Must ask the affected user to verify the production load pattern on a build containing the fix before declaring the issue resolved.
Must not conflate the later spinning-stream crashes reported after this issue was resolved with the original CPU-spike defect; maintainers explicitly treated them as a separate problem.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced production platform operator comfortable with HAProxy administration, BOSH deployments, perf, strace, socket CLI commands, HATop, anonymized diagnostic dumps, and fleet-wide version rollouts, but relies on maintainers to interpret HAProxy's internal task and connection flags.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, empirical, and cooperative; supplies raw logs and graphs, clearly distinguishes production from isolated tests, challenges hypotheses with fleet evidence, and avoids deploying experimental patches directly to production.
